description: We're Making an Interactive Mars MAP. We've used the Jezero Crater and NASA Data sets and we have already made the backend layer.
summary:
Martian Map is a 3D surface traverse planner and hazard-aware navigation system for Jezero Crater, Mars. Built on real orbital elevation data from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (20 m CTX DEM and 1 m HiRISE DTM) and NASA's Mars 2020 Perseverance and Ingenuity mission telemetry, the platform transforms raw planetary topography into an interactive 3D mission planning environment.

To address the challenge of safe Martian surface navigation, our engine computes local terrain slope (via Horn's method), surface roughness, and cliff-proximity hazard grids in true Martian meters. When users select start, goal, or multi-stop science waypoints, our routing engine (supporting Fast MCP, A*, and Dijkstra with any-angle Theta* path smoothing) simultaneously generates and compares three distinct traverses—Shortest, Balanced, and Safest—while strictly enforcing configurable slope limits and quantifying 3D distance, cumulative ascent/descent, travel time, and hazard exposure. We also validate our orbital terrain models directly against Perseverance's 45.3 km ground-truth traverse and rover tilt telemetry.

This tool is vital because future robotic sample recovery and crewed Martian EVA missions require rapid, transparent trade-offs between travel time, energy expenditure, and terrain safety before committing to a traverse.
details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

What it does:
Martian Map — Jezero Crater is an interactive, full-stack 3D planetary terrain visualization and kinematic rover route-planning platform designed for Jezero Crater, Mars (18.38° N, 77.69° E). Built using official orbital topography from the USGS Astrogeology Science Center (20-meter-per-pixel Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Context Camera Digital Elevation Model) and live localization telemetry from NASA and JPL’s Mars 2020 Perseverance Rover and Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, the platform allows mission planners, researchers, and students to explore Martian geology in 3D and compute terrain-aware surface traverses between any coordinates or multi-stop waypoints.

How it works:

  1. Orbital DEM Ingestion and Coordinate Transformation:
    On startup, the backend automatically verifies and ingests official USGS orbital elevation data (4,456 × 5,067 pixels covering 92 × 99 km) alongside NASA Mars 2020 Perseverance traverse and Sol waypoint datasets. All coordinates are mapped onto the IAU Mars 2000 sphere (with a mean radius of 3,396,190 meters) using latitude-corrected horizontal step scaling so that distance and slope calculations remain physically accurate.
  2. Terrain Intelligence and Hazard Derivation:
    From the raw elevation matrix, the engine applies Horn’s 3 × 3 finite-difference operator to compute local slope angles in degrees. It then calculates a 5 × 5 neighborhood slope standard deviation combined with a scarp-proximity buffer to generate a normalized Terrain Hazard Index ranging from 0 to 1.
    • Impassable Slope Blocking and Island Guard: The solver blocks any terrain cells that exceed the user’s configurable maximum rover slope threshold (adjustable from 5° to 40°, with a default of 25°) and uses Breadth-First Search (BFS) connected-component snapping so that start and goal points never become stranded on isolated mesa islands.
    • Convex Wheel-Slip and Directional Climb Penalties: The cost function models non-linear rocker-bogie wheel slip in loose Martian regolith using a quadratic slip curve, while also applying asymmetric gravitational climb penalties for steep uphill grades.
    • Simultaneous Three-Strategy Optimization: The engine computes three distinct routes in parallel—Shortest (optimizing pure geometric distance), Balanced (weighing distance against moderate slope and roughness avoidance), and Safest (maximizing clearance from steep grades, delta scarps, and rough bedrock)—and refines them using Any-Angle Theta* line-of-sight ray-marching to remove artificial 45° grid stair-stepping.
  3. High-Definition 3D WebGL Rendering and Barycentric Draping:
    The frontend renders a 420 × 420 vertex displacement mesh (176,400 vertices) complete with a 3D geologic cross-section pedestal base, dynamically synthesized albedo and tangent-space normal maps across six scientific surface modes, and exact barycentric triangle draping. This draping algorithm ensures that 3D route tubes and mission tracks conform tightly to crater bowls and ridge crests without clipping underground or floating in mid-air.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Install Browser Accessibility: The application replaces heavy desktop planetary GIS workflows—which traditionally require specialized tools like GDAL, ISIS3, QGIS, or ArcGIS—with an instant, hardware-accelerated 3D web interface that runs in any modern browser.
  • Side-by-Side Trade-Off Telemetry: Instead of returning a single black-box path, the platform simultaneously visualizes Shortest, Balanced, and Safest corridors and provides full comparative telemetry, including total distance in kilometers, drive duration in hours, cumulative ascent and descent in meters, maximum and mean slope angles, terrain hazard ratings, and interactive elevation profile charts.
  • Empirical Cross-Validation Against Real Mars Rover Telemetry: Our terrain slope and elevation models are directly validated against 708 actual NASA Perseverance Sol waypoints (spanning Sol 13 to Sol 2022 across 45.25 km of driving) using onboard Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) rover tilt logs. This validation achieves a strong Pearson correlation of 0.802, a Mean Absolute Error of 2.36°, and a median elevation offset of -0.87 meters.
  • Multi-Scale Spatial Inspection: Users can seamlessly switch between Full Crater (92 × 99 km), Crater Rim (61 × 55 km), and Delta & Rover (24 × 22 km) views while adjusting vertical exaggeration between 1x, 2.2x, and 3.5x to inspect subtle topographic features.
  • Integrated Mission Context: The 3D scene overlays the actual Perseverance traverse from touchdown (Sol 0) to the present, all 72 Ingenuity Mars Helicopter flights (17.0 km flown, rendered with 3D parabolic hop arcs), the Three Forks Mars Sample Return (MSR) Sample Depot, and 31 official IAU and USGS geological landmarks.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Bridging Static Orbital Data and Dynamic Surface Operations: The project demonstrates how public NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) and USGS Astrogeology orbital archives can be transformed from static 2D rasters into interactive decision-support tools for robotic and future human surface exploration.
  • Advancing Strategic Corridor Planning: While onboard rover navigation systems (such as Perseverance’s AutoNav and ENAV) handle local meter-scale hazard avoidance over 10-to-100-meter horizons, they rely on kilometer-scale strategic route planning to avoid regional topographic traps, box canyons, and high-slip scarps. Martian Map provides that strategic orbital-to-surface planning layer.
  • STEM Education and Public Engagement: The platform empowers students, educators, and space enthusiasts to step into the role of a Mars Rover planner—experimenting firsthand with how rover speed, slope limits, and geological formations (such as the Séítah olivine ridges or the Western Delta scarps) shape real-world exploration routes across an ancient Martian paleolake.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Development Workflow and AI Collaboration:
    Approximately 60% to 70% of the project was engineered directly in VS Code by the team—encompassing the core geospatial architecture, mathematical terrain modeling, kinematic pathfinding algorithms, and 3D scene engineering—while the remaining 30% to 40% was developed with the assistance of AI tools including AI Studio, Codex, Antigravity, and Claude Code for rapid prototyping, UI refinement, code optimization, and automated test generation.
  • Coding Languages:
    We used TypeScript and JavaScript (ES2022) for the full-stack web application, real-time 3D rendering, and in-memory GeoTIFF decoding and pathfinding engine; Python (3.11+) for the standalone scientific geospatial pipeline, batch analysis, API service, and empirical rover IMU telemetry validation; and HTML5 and CSS3 (with Tailwind CSS and custom glassmorphic styling) for the responsive three-column mission control interface and mobile drawers.
  • Frontend Frameworks and 3D Graphics Software:
    We built the user interface using React 19 and Vite 8 for modular component architecture and optimized bundle chunking. For 3D visualization, we used Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei to handle WebGL displacement mesh rendering, procedural normal and albedo texture synthesis, camera physics, and 3D polyline tube draping, alongside Zustand for global state management and Lucide React for technical iconography.
  • Backend and Geospatial Software Libraries:
    The backend runs on Node.js and Express 5 to serve REST API endpoints with automated dataset bootstrapping and Least Recently Used (LRU) memory caching. For geospatial processing, we used GeoTIFF libraries in JavaScript alongside Rasterio, GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj, pandas, and Matplotlib in Python to handle raster window decoding, bilinear resampling, Horn slope extraction, minimum-cost pathfinding, coordinate reprojection, and validation plotting.
  • Quality Assurance and Hardware:
    Development and testing were carried out in VS Code using the Node.js native test runner, Pytest, Oxlint, Prettier, and the TypeScript compiler. The platform was built and tested on standard workstation hardware utilizing WebGL2-capable GPU acceleration for client-side 1024 × 1024 shader and texture synthesis, paired with multi-core CPU execution for sub-second graph searches.

5. How is your project creative?

  1. Six Real-Time Procedural Scientific Surface Shaders From a Single DEM:
    Rather than forcing users to download gigabytes of pre-baked static image tiles, the browser dynamically synthesizes tangent-space normal maps, dual-azimuth hillshading (315° NW primary illumination with 255° WSW fill light), and Laplacian curvature on the fly to render six distinct scientific visualization modes:
    • Regolith HD: Photorealistic ferric and basaltic Martian soil shading with ridge sharpening.
    • MOLA Topo: Standard hypsometric elevation color ramp from deep basin greens to high peak whites.
    • Lithology & Carbonates: Geological unit mapping that highlights Marginal Carbonates along the -2,395 m paleolake shoreline, Fe/Mg-smectite delta clays, Séítah olivine-cumulate bedrock, and Máaz basaltic floor lavas.
    • Thermal Inertia: A physical rock consolidation proxy derived from local slope, curvature roughness, and equator-facing solar aspect.
    • CTX Orbital: High-contrast panchromatic Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Context Camera simulation.
    • Slope Hazard: A real-time rover traversability heatmap color-coded into safe green (0°–8°), caution amber (8°–20°), and impassable crimson (>20°) zones.
  2. Exact Barycentric Triangle Draping and Ridge Convexity Guard:
    In conventional 3D terrain viewers, polylines connecting two points across a crater or ridge often cut underground through terrain triangles or hover unnaturally in mid-air. We engineered an exact planar triangle intersection algorithm paired with a ridge convexity envelope that subdivides every route segment finer than 0.42 times a single DEM grid cell, ensuring that 3D route tubes hug every crater lip and valley floor accurately.
  3. Ground-Truthing Orbital Algorithms with Actual Martian Hardware:
    Rather than relying solely on theoretical simulations, we built an empirical validation pipeline that compares our orbital DEM slope calculations against Perseverance’s actual onboard IMU suspension tilt across 708 Sols. This quantifies exactly how 20-meter orbital pixels smooth out 3-meter rover-scale rocks and ripples on the Martian surface.
  4. Dual-Engine Resilience and Instant Analytic Fallback:
    The architecture combines a pure-TypeScript Node.js engine for zero-dependency cloud deployment with a Python scientific library for offline GIS research. In addition, an instant analytic Gaussian crater model renders immediately upon page load so the 3D viewport is interactive within milliseconds while the full USGS GeoTIFF streams in the background.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Physical Realism and Rover Kinematics:
    Planetary rovers cannot climb arbitrary grades or execute sharp 45° grid turns without experiencing wheel slip. Our team accounted for the angle of repose of Martian drift sand (approximately 25° to 30°), non-linear quadratic wheel-slip curves, asymmetric uphill energy expenditure, topological corner-cutting guards (which prevent diagonal paths from squeezing between two impassable boulders or scarps), and Any-Angle Theta* line-of-sight smoothing.
  • Planetary Cartography and Map Projections:
    At Jezero Crater’s latitude (approximately 18.44° N), an equirectangular degree of longitude is shorter than a degree of latitude by a factor of cos(18.44°), or roughly 0.9487. Both our TypeScript and Python engines explicitly account for the IAU Mars 2000 spherical reference body and local metric scaling so that slope gradients and route distances are scientifically accurate.
  • Computational Performance and Memory Efficiency:
    Running A* search across a full 4,456 × 5,067 raster (over 22.5 million cells) on every slider adjustment would freeze an interactive web application. To solve this, we implemented dynamic bounding-box sub-window cropping with adaptive safety margins, a 500,000-cell solver safety ceiling, typed-array binary min-heaps, and in-memory LRU caches to guarantee sub-second route recalculations.
  • 3D Camera Ergonomics and Anti-Collision Physics:
    Navigating high-relief 3D terrain frequently causes cameras to clip underground or lose their focal point during close-up inspection. We engineered a per-frame Camera Surface Guard that clamps both the camera eye position and orbit target strictly above the local triangle mesh height, paired with an auto-fading dynamic metric scale bar that continuously recalculates kilometers-per-pixel during zoom and orbit maneuvers.
  • Data Provenance and Open Science Licensing:
    Every dataset, scientific citation, and coordinate reference system used in the platform is grounded in authentic, public-domain NASA, JPL-Caltech, and USGS Astrogeology mission products and distributed under an open-source Apache 2.0 license.
